title: CSS History and the Move from One Specification to Modular Standards
learningObjectives: Describe the motivation for separating presentation from HTML document structure.
Identify the early proposal of CSS in 1994 and the publication of CSS1 as a W3C Recommendation in 1996.
Explain the significance of CSS2 becoming a Recommendation in 1998.
Describe why CSS3 did not become one single monolithic version release.
Explain the modular approach in which separate CSS specifications define features such as selectors, layout, colour and typography.
Identify modern CSS capabilities including Flexbox, Grid, custom properties, media queries and responsive design.
Explain how standards and browser implementations evolve together through specifications, tests and interoperability work.
Distinguish a specification publication date from browser support and real-world adoption.
Use current W3C CSS snapshots and module specifications to verify modern CSS features.
Summarize CSS evolution as a move from basic styling toward a broad, modular presentation and layout platform.

understand.concept: CSS was developed to separate presentation from HTML document structure. Håkon Wium Lie proposed CSS in 1994, and CSS1 became a W3C Recommendation in December 1996. CSS2 followed in 1998. As the language expanded, the CSS Working Group moved toward modular specifications: individual modules define areas such as selectors, layout, colour, fonts and animations. Modern CSS is therefore not best understood as one simple sequence of CSS3, CSS4 and CSS5 versions.
understand.whyItMatters: CSS history explains why the language supports reusable stylesheets and why its modern capabilities are spread across many specifications. It also helps developers find authoritative module documentation instead of relying on outdated version labels.
understand.analogy: CSS development is like a toolkit that began with a small set of tools and gradually gained specialized modules for different kinds of work.
understand.analogyLimit: The toolkit analogy does not show how modules interact through the cascade and rendering engine. A module can evolve independently, and browser support may differ while implementations and tests mature.
understand.history: The W3C records the CSS1 Recommendation on 17 December 1996 and CSS2 Recommendation in May 1998. W3C historical material describes the proposal work beginning in 1994. The current CSS Snapshot describes the state of CSS as a set of modules, rather than one monolithic version number.

explain.narrative:
CSS was proposed to address a problem: HTML was designed primarily to describe document structure, but authors also needed consistent control over fonts, colours, spacing and layout. Håkon Wium Lie began CSS proposal work in 1994, and Bert Bos joined the work. CSS1 became a W3C Recommendation on 17 December 1996. CSS2 became a Recommendation in May 1998.

The language then grew beyond what one document could conveniently describe. Instead of publishing one huge CSS3 specification and waiting for every feature to be finished, the CSS Working Group developed separate modules. Different modules cover selectors, values, colour, fonts, layout, transforms, animations and many other areas. This lets parts of CSS evolve at different rates.

Modern CSS includes capabilities such as Flexbox and Grid for layout, media queries for responsive and preference-aware design, custom properties for reusable values, and more powerful selectors. These are not all features of one single version called CSS4. They belong to modules with their own specifications and maturity levels.

When using a CSS feature, consult the relevant module documentation and current browser support. A published specification explains intended behaviour; browser testing confirms what users can rely on. The W3C CSS Snapshot is useful for understanding the current collection of CSS specifications.

examples.code: CSS rules evolve over time.
examples.explanation: Change the style rule and observe how colour, spacing and layout change.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays the HTML content according to the CSS declarations.

examples.title: Selected CSS standards milestones
examples.code:
1994  CSS proposal work begins
1996  CSS1 becomes a W3C Recommendation
1998  CSS2 becomes a W3C Recommendation
Later CSS  Modular specifications evolve separately
Today CSS Snapshot summarizes the current module landscape
examples.explanation: The milestones show the shift from a small stylesheet specification to a broad family of modules. They do not imply that all browsers supported every feature immediately.
examples.expectedOutput: You can describe the early milestones and explain the modern modular approach.

examples.title: Modern CSS is a family of modules
examples.code:
Selectors → how elements are matched
Values & Units → property values and calculations
Flexbox / Grid → layout systems
Media Queries → viewport and user preferences
Color / Fonts → visual presentation
Animations → time-based visual changes
examples.explanation: Each area has its own specification work and browser implementation history. Use the module that defines the feature you need rather than searching for one universal CSS version.
examples.expectedOutput: A map of different CSS capabilities and their specification areas.

examples.title: Check feature maturity and compatibility
examples.code:
Before adopting a CSS feature:
1. Find its module specification.
2. Check the feature's maturity/status.
3. Review browser support for target users.
4. Test fallback behaviour.
5. Verify accessibility and responsive results.
examples.explanation: A feature's appearance in a draft or snapshot does not automatically mean it is safe for every target browser. Compatibility decisions depend on the product's support policy.

practise.guidedTask: Build a timeline of the CSS milestones and identify which capabilities belong to modern modules. Choose Grid or a media query and locate its specification and browser support information.
practise.independentTask: Write a short technical note comparing CSS1's original purpose with modern modular CSS. Include three modules you use in a project, their purpose and how you would verify support in target browsers.
hints: CSS was proposed in 1994 and CSS1 became a Recommendation in 1996.
Modern CSS is modular; avoid claiming CSS4 is one complete unified standard.
A specification date is not the same as a browser support date.
Use W3C module documentation and compatibility data.

questions.prompt: In which year did CSS1 become a W3C Recommendation?
questions.explanation: Keep the roles of HTML structure and CSS presentation distinct.

questions.prompt: Does using CSS remove the need for semantic HTML?
questions.explanation: HTML provides meaning and structure; CSS controls presentation.

questions.prompt: When did CSS1 become a W3C Recommendation?
questions.explanation: W3C published the CSS1 Recommendation on 17 December 1996.

questions.prompt: Why is modern CSS described as modular?
options: Different feature areas are defined and developed in separate specifications.
Every CSS property belongs to a different programming language.
CSS no longer has a cascade.
questions.answer: Different feature areas are defined and developed in separate specifications.
questions.explanation: Selectors, layout, colour, fonts and other areas have their own modules and development status.

questions.prompt: What should you check before relying on a new CSS feature?
options: Its specification, browser support and fallback needs.
Only the year the feature was proposed.
Only the colour of the browser toolbar.
questions.answer: Its specification, browser support and fallback needs.
questions.explanation: Standards and browser compatibility evidence help determine whether a feature is suitable for the target environment.
